en: What it doesn't show: This does not reproduce any real city's road network. It is this project's simplified model: a small symmetric network, everyone with the same origin and destination, drivers who care only about time, and the same choices repeated day after day. It does not mean shortcuts or new roads are always harmful, nor that roads should not be built: with light traffic the shortcut clearly helped. Stories from places such as Stuttgart or Seoul's Cheonggyecheon, where closing or removing a road supposedly improved traffic, are often cited as examples of this paradox, but they are mixed with other changes in traffic, so the evidence is anecdotal, and this model neither explains nor reproduces those events. Reality also involves things this model leaves out, such as switching to public transport, changing departure times, and induced demand where a new road brings new traffic.

This project's own implementation illustrating the paradox described in Braess (1968), "Über ein Paradoxon aus der Verkehrsplanung", Unternehmensforschung 12, 258-268. It does not reproduce that paper's numbers; the setting of 4,000 drivers, x/100 minutes on congestible roads and a fixed 45 minutes follows the widely used textbook example (Easley & Kleinberg, Networks, Crowds, and Markets).

Treating drivers as a continuous quantity, the equilibrium can be solved in closed form. With a = sensitivity/1000, fixed time 45 and shortcut cost c: if a × drivers + c ≤ 45 everyone takes the shortcut and the average is 2a × drivers + c; if it is more crowded but a × drivers < 2(45 − c), only some take it and all three routes tie at 90 − c; beyond that nobody takes it, same as closed. Graphs ④ and ⑤ use these formulas, and I checked that the end state of the simulation matches them.

For linear delays (a congestible road's time proportional to its drivers), Roughgarden & Tardos (2002), "How bad is selfish routing?", Journal of the ACM 49(2) show that the selfish equilibrium is at most 4/3 times worse than the social optimum. In this model the price of anarchy peaks at 1.33 (4/3) with 4,500 drivers (cost 0, sensitivity 10), equal to that bound.

You can verify with node tools/validate-braess.js. The simulation uses a seeded random generator (mulberry32), so the same seed gives the same result. The social optimum is the minimum average time found by trying every possible number of shortcut users one by one.
The code is available on GitHub.
Is a Coincidence Not a Coincidence? · Simulatio Lab
A spooky coincidence is often stranger when it never happens. Use the birthday problem to see how different "a match somewhere" is from "a match with me".

Learning that two people in a gathering share a birthday gives you a chill: "this can't be chance". Yet with only a few people in the room, it would be stranger if nothing like it happened. Change the headcount, the number of features and the size of each feature, and watch how "someone matches somewhere" differs from "someone matches me".

N people gather in a room. Everyone has k features: the first is a birthday (365 values, leap days ignored) and the others are things like hometown, hobby or school, each with a fixed number of possible values. All are drawn independently with equal chances.
Two people who share at least one feature form a matching pair. N people make N(N−1)/2 possible pairs: when the headcount grows N-fold, the pairs grow roughly N²-fold.
Person 0 is me. The model counts separately "a match somewhere in the room" and "someone matches me". Lines are calculated values (theory) and dots are results of actually running many gatherings.

The model assumes every feature is uniform and independent. Real birthdays are not perfectly even through the year, and people from the same hometown may share hobbies, so reality is more complicated.

What it shows: With birthday only (one feature), the chance that some pair in the room shares a birthday was 50.7% with 23 people and 99.0% with 57 people (running 20,000 gatherings gave 50.4% and 99.0%, matching the calculation). Among 23 people there are as many as 253 possible pairs. But the chance that someone shares a birthday with me was only 5.9% with the same 23 people and just 14.2% with 57, and to pass 50% it took 253 people besides me (254 in all). The same 23 people give 50.7% for "someone, somewhere" and 5.9% for "me". Adding features makes "somewhere" nearly certain very quickly. With 23 people and features of birthday plus one 30-value feature (2 features), the chance of some match was above 99.999%, effectively 100% and the chance of matching me rose to 55.3%. With 3 features the chance of matching me was 78.8%, and with 6 features it was 97.7%. A striking coincidence needs only "any match at all", not "the specific match I picked in advance", so wherever people gather, some match turns up somewhere. The statisticians Diaconis and Mosteller (1989) called this the "law of truly large numbers": with a large enough sample, even very rare events happen somewhere.
